lesson.title: The Dative Case
lesson.subtitle: The giving case: mir↔me, dir↔thee, ihm↔him — and the methinks fossils

payoff.text: Remember sprig 1003 leaving this open: 'you have not met the case that moves die either.' Here it is. 'To her' is ihr, and when an article has to mean 'to the lady', it is still D- + the pronoun: D- + ihr = der. So die Frau becomes der Frau — not because someone changed a table, but because the case changed which pronoun the D- is holding.

hook.title: The Case of the Receiver
hook.content: The accusative marks what gets acted on. The dative marks who gets the result — the receiver. Ich gebe ihm das Buch: I give the book TO HIM. English once wore this case openly: 'Give it ME' (the archaic British phrasing), 'methinks' ('it thinks TO ME'), 'I give it THEE'. German never stopped: mir (to me), dir (to thee), ihm (to him) — each one a twin of an English fossil. And a whole club of German verbs demands the dative: helfen, danken, gefallen. You do not 'help someone' in German — you help TO someone.

footnotes.title: Methinks, the Dative Fossil
footnotes.content: Methinks is not 'me thinking' — it is 'it seems TO ME' (OE mē þyncþ), the dative experiencer. German still says the same thing the same way: Mir ist kalt is 'it is cold TO ME'. English buried the dative; German made it a lifestyle.

pattern.title: The Receiver's Toolbox
pattern.content:
The pronouns first: mir ↔ me (to me), dir ↔ thee (to thee), ihm ↔ him (to him) — the same words with the same ancient jobs. The prepositions that always drag the dative along: aus (out of), bei (by — the exact twin of by), mit (with — the twin of mid, as in midwife), nach (after), seit (since), von (from), zu (to). The dative verbs: helfen (Ich helfe dir), danken (Ich danke dir — you already said it!), gefallen (Es gefällt mir — it falls well to me), geben (Gib mir das Buch). When both objects appear, English word order does the dative's job ('give HIM the book'); German marks it on the words: gib ihm das Buch — ihm = to-him (dative), das Buch = accusative.

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Gib ihm das Buch → Give to-him the book → Give him the book. The middle line shows the case on the page: the 'to' lives inside ihm.
pattern.linguist_note: The dative articles: dem (masculine/neuter), der (feminine), den (+ -n) in the plural. Notice dem keeps the ancient m, while the accusative softened it to n (ihn, wen) — one nasal, two case stories.

exercises.prompt: Match the dative pronouns with their English twins:
exercises.meaning: to me, to thee, to him, with
exercises.explanation: The dative pronouns are English fossils alive in German: 'give it me', 'I give it thee', 'give it him' — plus mit/mid.

exercises.meaning: Ich danke dir = I thank thee
exercises.explanation: danken demands the dative — thanking goes TO someone. dich would be the accusative; danken refuses it.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.explanation: German keeps the 'to' audible inside the dative pronoun — ihm IS 'to him'. English used to say 'give it me'; German never stopped.

exercises.prompt: Give it to me: 'Gib _____ das Buch!' (to me):
exercises.english_hint: the archaic 'give it me' — dative of ich
exercises.meaning: Gib mir das Buch = Give me the book
exercises.explanation: The receiver takes the dative: mir — the same case English fossilized in 'give it me'.

exercises.idea: a friend is carrying something heavy: you offer the ancient verb — I help thee
cues: helfen is a dative verb: the help goes TO someone — ich helfe dir
exercises.explanation: helfen + dative: 'Ich helfe dir' — help goes TO the person, as English once said 'I help thee' with a to.

diagnosis.slip: the dative verb was fed an accusative
diagnosis.cue: helfen refuses the Him-Case: ich helfe dir (to-thee), never 'ich helfe dich'. Helping goes TO someone.

summary.outcome: Use mir, dir, ihm and the dative verbs helfen, danken, gefallen correctly.
summary.takeaway: The dative marks the receiver: mir/dir/ihm ↔ 'give it me/thee/him' — and helfen, danken, gefallen demand it.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: methinks & Dative Survivors — the English dative fossils mirrored in German, dem/den/dem grid row.

twist.prompt: Same verb, different receiver: I help thee becomes I help HIM. (The dative pronoun has three faces.)
twist.explanation: dir → ihm: both dative, both English fossils ('give it thee' → 'give it him'). ihn would be the accusative — helfen refuses it.

mir.context_translation: Can you please help me? (literally: help to me)
mir.etymology_derivation: Dative of ich — the same ancient pronoun as English me, keeping the 'to me' meaning (mir ist kalt = it is cold to me). [wiktionary]

dir.etymology_derivation: Dative of du — the exact twin of archaic English 'I give it thee'; the dative is the giving case. [wiktionary]

ihm.etymology_derivation: Dative of er — the exact twin of English him; the h dropped from speech and stayed in spelling. [wiktionary]

mit.etymology_derivation: The exact twin of archaic English mid 'with' — fossilized in midwife, 'with-woman'. Governs the dative. [wiktionary]

bei.etymology_derivation: The exact twin of English by — both from Proto-Germanic *bi. Governs the dative. [wiktionary]

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

gefallen.context_translation: I like it (it falls well to me).
gefallen.etymology_derivation: ge- + fallen — 'to fall to someone' (by lot or liking), like English 'as it falls out'. Strong verb: gefiel, gefallen. [wiktionary]

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

euro.etymology_derivation: Clipping of Europa — the same root as English Europe. [wiktionary]

luft.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *luftuz; Old English lyft and Icelandic loft compared, modern twin unconfirmed. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

sauer.etymology_derivation: sauer — from Proto-Germanic *sūraz, PIE *súHros, the exact cognate of English sour; the long ū diphthongized to au in both languages. [wiktionary]

gewitter.context_phrase: Bei dem Gewitter bleiben wir drinnen.
gewitter.context_translation: During the thunderstorm we stay inside.
gewitter.etymology_derivation: Ge- plus Wetter (weather) — literally an intensified weather; from Proto-Germanic *gawidriją, the same root as English weather, which the page notes is distantly cognate in structure to English aweather. [wiktionary]

welt.context_phrase: Die Welt ist groß und schön.
welt.context_translation: The world is big and beautiful.
welt.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Old High German wëralt, from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz, literally the age of man. English world is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

langeweile.etymology_derivation: lang (long) + Weile (while — the exact English cognate): boredom is a long while. [wiktionary]

fall.context_phrase: In diesem Fall nehme ich den Bus.
fall.context_translation: In this case I take the bus.
fall.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fall — English fall is the documented cognate; the grammar sense (in diesem Fall) is a calque of Latin casus. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
